parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: When the growth factor (the ligand) binds its receptor, the receptor changes shape and becomes active. This starts a signal transduction pathway, for example phosphorylation cascades through relay proteins or kinases. The pathway activates transcription factors that turn on genes for cell-cycle proteins such as cyclins and Cdks, so the cell passes the G1 checkpoint and divides.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: (i) The independent variable is the growth factor concentration (ng/mL). The dependent variable is the percent of cells in mitosis after 24 hours. (ii) One factor to keep constant is temperature (other options: culture medium/nutrients, cell type, incubation time, starting cell density, CO2 level). (iii) As the growth factor concentration goes up, the mean percent of cells in mitosis rises, from 4.0% at 0 ng/mL to 17.1% at 20 ng/mL. The increase gets smaller at higher concentrations (+5.1 from 0 to 5, +4.5 from 5 to 10, +3.5 across the larger step from 10 to 20).

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: (i) Percent change = (17.1 − 4.0)/4.0 × 100 = 13.1/4.0 × 100 = 327.5% (about a 328% increase). (ii) The ±2SE range at 5 ng/mL is 8.14–10.06, and at 10 ng/mL it is 12.64–14.56. The ranges do not overlap, so the difference between the two means is statistically supported.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The percent of cells in mitosis would drop below 17.1%, likely to near the 0 ng/mL level of about 4%. The blocked receptor cannot bind the growth factor, so the signaling pathway that drives cell division is not activated, even though plenty of growth factor is present.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: Bristle number is heritable and varies among flies. Only flies with the most bristles reproduce, so the alleles linked to high bristle number are passed on more often. These alleles become more common in each generation, and the population mean goes up.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: (i) The independent variable is the number of generations of selective breeding. The dependent variable is the number of bristles per fly (the mean). (ii) Factors to keep constant include temperature, food or medium, the starting population and strain, how old the flies are when counted, sex, and the sample size. (iii) The mean bristle number goes up as generations increase, from 34.0 to 37.0 to 45.6 to 52.5. The rise is small between 0 and 3 generations and larger after that.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: (i) (52.5 − 34.0)/34.0 × 100 ≈ 54.4% increase. (ii) The interval at 3 generations is 34.32–39.68 and the interval at 6 generations is 42.84–48.36. The ±2SE intervals do not overlap, so the difference is statistically supported.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The mean would stay at about 34 bristles, close to the starting value. Without selection, flies with high and low bristle numbers reproduce about equally. Allele frequencies would not shift in one direction, apart from small random changes from drift.
parts.issue: The reference says 'about 35', but the starting value is 34.0. The difference is small and falls within the 0-generation error range, so the answer is still acceptable.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: As the drug concentration goes up, the mean percent of cells in mitosis goes down: 11.9% at 0 µM, 7.0% at 5 µM and 2.4% at 20 µM. The highest value is at 0 µM and the lowest is at 20 µM.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: Percent change = ((2.4 − 11.9) / 11.9) × 100 = (−9.5 / 11.9) × 100 ≈ −79.8%. This is a decrease of about 80%.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: The ±2SE ranges are 11.08–12.72 at 0 µM, 6.40–7.60 at 5 µM and 2.14–2.66 at 20 µM. The 0 µM range does not overlap either of the other two ranges, so the difference is likely statistically significant in both comparisons. The data support the claim.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The drug could stop cells at a checkpoint before mitosis, such as G1/S or G2/M, for example by blocking cyclin/CDK activity. The cells would then build up in interphase. Because fewer cells move into mitosis, a smaller fraction of the culture is in mitosis at any one time.

parts.label: (A)
parts.your_answer: As the mice get older, the mean percent of eggs with an abnormal number of chromosomes goes up: 2.0% at 3 months, 9.2% at 12 months and 28.5% at 18 months. The rise is steeper later on, with a gain of 7.2 points from 3 to 12 months and 19.3 points from 12 to 18 months.

parts.label: (B)
parts.your_answer: Percent change = ((28.5 − 2.0) / 2.0) × 100 = (26.5 / 2.0) × 100 = 1325%, which is an increase.

parts.label: (C)
parts.your_answer: The ±2SE ranges are 25.12–31.88 at 18 months, 1.80–2.20 at 3 months and 8.30–10.10 at 12 months. The 18-month range does not overlap either of the other two ranges, so the data support the claim. The mean at 18 months is likely higher than both other means.

parts.label: (D)
parts.your_answer: Nondisjunction happens when homologous chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis I, or sister chromatids fail to separate in meiosis II. One daughter cell then gets an extra chromosome (n+1) and another gets one too few (n−1). If the egg is the cell with the wrong number, it is aneuploid.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: Second order in A. The values of 1/[A] are 1.000, 2.200, 3.400, 4.600, 5.800 and 6.998 M^-1, which rise by about 1.20 M^-1 every 30 s. So a plot of 1/[A] against t is a straight line. The ln[A] plot (0, -0.788, -1.224, -1.526, -1.758, -1.946) curves, and so does the plot of [A] against t. That rules out first and zero order.

parts.label: B
parts.issue: The reference writes |slope|. For a 1/[A] plot the slope is already positive, so the absolute value bars are unnecessary but do no harm.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: k increases. At a higher temperature the particles move faster, so they collide more often. More importantly, a larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to Ea, so more collisions are successful.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: First order. Each 30 s interval keeps the same ratio, [A]t/[A]0 ≈ 0.6376, so the half-life is constant. Plot ln[A] against time. The plot is a straight line with a negative slope, while plots of [A] vs t and 1/[A] vs t curve.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: t1/2 = 0.693/0.0150 s⁻¹ ≈ 46 s (46.2 s). For a first-order reaction this value does not depend on the starting concentration.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: k increases. At a higher temperature, molecules move faster and collide more often. More importantly, a larger fraction of collisions have energy equal to or greater than Ea, so more collisions succeed per unit time.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: MP of the 3rd worker = 70 − 52 = 18 chairs. MRP = 18 × $3 = $54.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: MRP1 = 30×3 = $90, MRP2 = 22×3 = $66, MRP3 = $54. The firm hires while MRP ≥ $55, so it hires 2 workers.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: Worker 3's MRP ($54) is less than the wage ($55). Hiring that worker adds more to cost than to revenue, so profit would fall by $1.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: Labor demand (MRP = MP × P) increases and shifts right, because a higher product price raises MRP at every quantity of labor.

parts.label: E
parts.your_answer: Fewer. A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply curve, so to hire one more worker it must raise the wage for all its workers. That makes MFC greater than the wage. It hires where MRP = MFC, which is fewer workers than where MRP = the wage (supply).

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: For each additional hour of study, the predicted exam score goes up by about 4.81 points.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: No. The plot is curved. The points lie above the line at both ends (x=1 is about +31.7; x=9 is about +11 to +17). They lie below the line in the middle (x=3 to 8, e.g. about −18 at x=5). Residuals with a clear curved pattern mean a linear model is not appropriate.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: About 47% of the variation in exam score is explained by the linear relationship with hours of study.

parts.label: E
parts.your_answer: No. x = 17 is far outside the observed range of hours (1 to 9), so this is extrapolation. The relationship may not hold there, and the data already look curved.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: For each additional hour of study, the predicted exam score increases by about 5.2 points.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: Yes. The residuals are scattered above and below the line across the whole x-range with no curved pattern. The point (8, 76.2) has a large negative residual (about −9.9), but there is no systematic pattern, so a linear model is appropriate.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: About 94% of the variation in exam score is explained by the linear relationship with hours of study.

parts.label: E

parts.label: (a)
parts.your_answer: f is concave up on (4,8) because f' is increasing there. The slopes of the segments are 2 on both (4,6) and (6,8). On (0,4), f' is decreasing.

parts.label: (b)
parts.your_answer: At x=2, f' changes from positive to negative, so f has a relative maximum there. At x=6, f' changes from negative to positive, so f has a relative minimum there.

parts.label: (c)
parts.your_answer: f(2) = 1 + 2 = 3, f(6) = 3 - 8 = -5 and f(8) = -5 + 4 = -1. Comparing these with f(0) = 1, the absolute minimum is at x = 6.

parts.label: (a)
parts.your_answer: f is concave up on (4,8), because f' is increasing there (the segments from (4,-4) to (6,0) and from (6,0) to (8,4) both have positive slope).

parts.label: (b)
parts.your_answer: Relative maximum at x = 2, because f' changes from positive to negative there. Relative minimum at x = 6, because f' changes from negative to positive there.

parts.label: (c)
parts.your_answer: The candidates are the critical points and the endpoints. Using areas: f(2) = 3 + 2 = 5, f(6) = 5 − 8 = −3, f(8) = −3 + 4 = 1, and f(0) = 3. The smallest value is −3, so the absolute minimum is at x = 6.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: A competitive inhibitor looks like the substrate and binds to the enzyme's active site. This blocks the substrate from binding, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and the reaction slows down.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: (i) The independent variable is the concentration of compound X (µM). The dependent variable is the initial reaction rate (µmol of product per minute). (ii) One factor to keep constant is temperature. pH, substrate concentration or enzyme concentration would also work. (iii) As the concentration of compound X goes up, the mean initial rate goes down: from 40.7 at 0 µM to 11.8 at 8 µM.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: (i) Percent change = (11.8 − 40.7)/40.7 × 100 = −71.0%, a decrease of about 71%. (ii) The range at 2 µM is 28.8 ± 2.38, or 26.42 to 31.18. The range at 4 µM is 20.1 ± 2.18, or 17.92 to 22.28. The two ranges do not overlap, so the difference between the means is statistically supported.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: With much more substrate, compound X would have a smaller inhibitory effect, and the rate would get closer to the rate without the inhibitor. This is because substrate molecules outcompete the inhibitor for the active sites, so more active sites end up holding substrate.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: Water potential (Ψ) is the potential energy of water per unit volume, set by solute concentration (solute potential) and pressure (pressure potential). Water moves from higher to lower water potential.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: Line graph. Sucrose molarity (M) goes on the x-axis and percent change in mass (%) on the y-axis, with even scales that include negative values. Plot all six points and connect them; they fall on a straight decreasing line.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: (i) The data are linear (11.2 − 32M), so the line crosses 0% at about 0.35 M. (ii) Null hypothesis: sucrose molarity has no effect on the percent change in mass of the potato cores.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: In 0.4 M NaCl the cores would lose more mass than in 0.4 M sucrose. NaCl splits into two ions (i = 2), so the solution has about twice as many solute particles. That makes its solute potential (−iCRT), and so its water potential, more negative, and more water leaves the cores. The effect would be roughly like 0.8 M sucrose (about −14%).

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: The bottom template strand. It runs 3' to 5' from left to right, so a new strand made 5' to 3' grows continuously toward the right, the same way the fork moves.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: DNA polymerase only adds nucleotides to the 3' end. On the top template the new strand has to be built away from the fork, so synthesis starts again in short Okazaki fragments as more template is unwound.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: 3'-GCGATCTTA-5' (left end 3', right end 5')

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The new strand stays paired with the original top template strand, so each daughter molecule has one parental strand and one new strand. That is semiconservative replication.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: The bottom template strand (3' on the left, 5' on the right). Its new strand runs 5' to 3' from left to right, so it grows continuously toward the fork as the fork moves right.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only to a 3' end, so new DNA is made only 5' to 3'. On the top template, the new strand has to be made right to left, away from the moving fork. Synthesis therefore keeps restarting near the fork as new template is exposed, which produces short Okazaki fragments that are later joined by ligase.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: 3'-CCACCCACCG-5' (left end is 3', right end is 5')

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The new strand base-pairs with the original top template strand. The daughter double helix is therefore made of one parental (conserved) strand and one newly made strand, which is what semiconservative replication means.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: A change in the nucleotide sequence (a substitution, insertion or deletion) changes the mRNA codons made from the gene. This can put a different amino acid into the protein, cause a frameshift or create an early stop codon. A different amino-acid sequence can change how the protein folds, and so its shape and function.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: Independent variable: how long the cells are exposed to UV light (0, 10, 20 or 30 s). Dependent variable: the number of colonies (antibiotic-resistant cells) that grow on the antibiotic plates.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: Longer UV exposure will produce more colonies on the antibiotic plates. The 0 s plate should have few or no colonies.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: UV light damages DNA, for example by forming thymine dimers. When the damage is repaired wrongly or copied during replication, it causes mutations. Longer exposure causes more mutations, so more cells are likely to get a mutation in a gene that makes them resistant to the antibiotic. Because most cells survive, more resistant colonies grow.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: As drug concentration goes up, the mean percent of cells in mitosis goes down: 12.2% at 0 µM, 7.2% at 5 µM and 2.5% at 20 µM.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: The ±2SE ranges are 11.28–13.12 at 0 µM, 6.44–7.96 at 5 µM and 2.30–2.70 at 20 µM. The 0 µM range does not overlap either of the other two ranges, so the data support the claim for both comparisons.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: If the drug stops cells at a checkpoint before mitosis (for example, the G2/M checkpoint), cells stay in interphase and do not enter mitosis. That lowers the share of cells in mitosis at any given time.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: The MRPs are $78, $66, $54, $42 and $30. The firm keeps hiring while MRP ≥ $63, so it hires 2 workers.

parts.your_answer: Worker 3's MRP is $54, which is less than the $63 wage. Hiring that worker would cost more than the revenue the worker adds, so profit would fall.

parts.your_answer: Demand for labor increases (the curve shifts right). A higher output price raises MRP = MP × P at every quantity of labor.

parts.issue: No supply schedule is given, but the standard conceptual answer (fewer) still holds.
